The interior of charged black holes and the problem of uniqueness in general relativity

Mihalis Dafermos
Abstract

We consider a spherically symmetric double characteristic initial value problem for the Einstein-Maxwell-(real) scalar field equations. On the initial outgoing characteristic, the data is assumed to satisfy the Price law decay widely believed to hold on an event horizon arising from the collapse of an asymptotically flat Cauchy surface. We establish that the heuristic mass inflation scenario put forth by Israel and Poisson is mathematically correct in the context of this initial value problem. In particular, the maximal future development has a future boundary, over which the spacetime is extendible as a C0C^{0} metric, but along which the Hawking mass blows up identically; thus, the spacetime is inextendible as a C1C^{1} metric. In view of recent results of the author in collaboration with I. Rodnianski, which rigorously establish the validity of Price’s law as an upper bound for the decay of scalar field hair, the C0C^{0} extendibility result applies to the collapse of complete asymptotically flat spacelike initial data where the scalar field is compactly supported. This shows that under Christodoulou’s C0C^{0} formulation, the strong cosmic censorship conjecture is false for this system.

1 Introduction

The fact that the initial value problem for the Einstein equations is locally well-posed connects general relativity to the classical 19th-century physics of fields, and to the theory of equations of evolution in general. At first, it may seem that this also casts the theory squarely into the sphere of Newtonian determinism, the principle that initial data determine uniquely the solution. In quasilinear hyperbolic equations, however, such as the Einstein equations, where uniqueness is controlled by the a priori unknown global geometry of the characteristics, it is not immediate that one can pass from “local” to “global” determinism. In fact, it is well known that the Einstein equations allow for smooth Cauchy horizons to emerge in evolution from complete initial data, i.e. uniqueness may fail without any loss of regularity in the solution. This behavior indeed occurs in the celebrated Kerr solution; also in the spherically-symmetric Reissner-Nordström solution, as can be seen most easily by examining its so-called Penrose diagram11 1 See [24].:

In more physical language, our ability to predict the future from initial conditions on the complete Cauchy surface 𝒮\mathcal{S}, in particular the fate of the observer depicted above by the timelike geodesic γ\gamma, fails, as γ\gamma “exits” the domain of dependence of 𝒮\mathcal{S} in finite proper time. This failure, however, is not accompanied by any sort of blow up, as measured by γ\gamma, which would indicate that classical relativity should no longer apply.

The physical problems arising from this “loss of determinism” would be resolved if the phenomenon turned out to be unstable, i.e. if for generic initial data, uniqueness does indeed hold as long as the solution remains regular. The conjecture that this is the case, due to Penrose, goes by the name of strong cosmic censorship. Definite formulations are given in [24, 22, 13, 19].

The strong cosmic censorship conjecture was motivated by arguments of first order perturbation theory, indicating that the Cauchy horizon 𝒞​ℋ+\mathcal{CH}^{+} in a spherically symmetric Reissner-Nordström background is indeed unstable. The rigorous study of the stability of the Reissner-Nordström Cauchy horizon in a nonlinear p.d.e. setting was initiated in [22]. A certain spherically symmetric characteristic initial value problem was considered for the Einstein-Maxwell-scalar field22 2 The considerations leading to this particular system are discussed at length in [22, 23, 4, 5]. It is the analogy between the repulsive mechanism of charge and angular momentum which makes it possible to study the formation and instability of Cauchy horizons while remaining in the context of spherical symmetry. For the case where Fα​β=0F_{\alpha\beta}=0, the reader should consult [11, 12, 15, 17]. equations:

Rα​β−12​R​gα​β=2​Tα​β,R_{\alpha\beta}-\frac{1}{2}Rg_{\alpha\beta}=2T_{\alpha\beta}, (1)
F,αα​β=0,F[α​β,γ]=0,F^{,\alpha}_{\alpha\beta}=0,F_{[\alpha\beta,\gamma]}=0, (2)
gα​βϕ;αβ=0,g^{\alpha\beta}\phi_{;\alpha\beta}=0, (3)
Tα​β=ϕ;αϕ;β−12gα​βϕ;γϕ;γ+Fα​γFγβ−14gα​βFγδFδγ,T_{\alpha\beta}=\phi_{;\alpha}\phi_{;\beta}-\frac{1}{2}g_{\alpha\beta}\phi^{;\gamma}\phi_{;\gamma}+F_{\alpha\gamma}F^{\gamma}_{\ \beta}-\frac{1}{4}g_{\alpha\beta}F^{\gamma}_{\ \delta}F^{\delta}_{\ \gamma}, (4)

and it was proven that the maximal development of initial data has future boundary a Cauchy horizon over which the spacetime is extendible as a C0C^{0} metric. On the other hand, given an appropriate additional assumption on the initial data, it was shown that the Hawking mass blows up identically along this Cauchy horizon, and thus the spacetime is inextendible as a C1C^{1} metric.

The generic occurrence of a C1C^{1}-singular (but C0C^{0}-regular!) Cauchy horizon in the interior of spherically symmetric charged black holes arising from gravitational collapse was first conjectured by W. Israel and E. Poisson [34] on the basis of heuristic considerations; they termed this phenomenon mass inflation. Although several numerical [5, 6] studies subsequently confirmed the mass inflation scenario, it remained somewhat controversial, as it is at odds with the original picture put forth by Penrose, which had suggested the generic occurrence of a spacelike C0C^{0}-singular surface, terminating at i+i^{+}, rather than a null C1C^{1}-singular Cauchy horizon.

The results of [22] showed that in principle mass inflation could occur for solutions of the Einstein-Maxwell-scalar field system; the scenario was thus not an artifice of the Israel-Poisson heuristics. The results of [22] could not show, however, whether the scenario actually occurred for the collapse of generic asymptotically flat spacelike initial data. The initial outgoing null characteristic considered in [22] was meant to represent the event horizon of a black hole that had already formed. Moreover, to simplify the problem as much as possible, the assumptions imposed on the event horizon were very strong, in particular, the event horizon was required not to carry incoming scalar field radiation. This implied that it geometrically coincided with a Reissner-Nordström event horizon, and thus was at the same time an apparent horizon, i.e. it was foliated by marginally trapped spheres. The event horizon of a black hole arising from gravitational collapse, however, will in general have a qualitatively different structure from that of the Reissner-Nordström event horizon. It will not be foliated by marginally trapped spheres, and it will possess a radiating decaying scalar field “tail”. Heuristic analysis [26, 1, 2, 3] going back to Price [35], together with more recent numerical results [27, 8, 31], have indicated that, in the case of massless scalar field matter, this tail will decay polynomially with exponent −3-3, with respect to a naturally defined advanced time coordinate. This decay rate is widely known as Price’s law.

In the present paper, we demonstrate that results analogous to those of [22] can be established for data satisfying a weak form of the conjectured Price law decay discussed above.33 3 In particular, this data includes the intial data considered in the numerical studies [5, 6]. To state the theorems, it will be helpful to apply the standard notation of Penrose diagrams. The reader can refer to [24]. In particular the labelled subsets 𝒞​ℋ+\mathcal{CH}^{+}, ℐ+\mathcal{I}^{+}, i+i^{+}, ℋ+\mathcal{H}^{+} acquire a well-defined meaning from their position in the diagram.

The second main result of the paper is

Theorem 1.2.

Let p>12p>\frac{1}{2}, and C,c,ϵ>0C,c,\epsilon>0. Consider data as in Theorem 1.1, where in place of (5)(\ref{avtitoumavva}), we assume

When the above results were first obtained, the only motivation for the assumptions was the heuristic and numerical evidence mentioned above. In view of recent work [24] of the author in collaboration with I. Rodnianski, however, it follows now that the assumptions of Theorem 1.1, in fact the stronger bound,

|∂vϕ|≤Cϵ​v−3+ϵ,|\partial_{v}\phi|\leq C_{\epsilon}v^{-3+\epsilon}, (6)

for any ϵ>0\epsilon>0, indeed hold on the event horizon of black holes arising from the collapse of general complete spherically symmetric asymptotically flat spacelike data for which the charge is non-zero44 4 The reader should note that in the case of non-vanishing charge, complete spherically symmetric Cauchy data necessarily will have two asymptotically flat ends, and this easily implies that trapped surfaces occur and thus an event horizon necessarily forms. See [21]., and the scalar field is compactly supported55 5 In fact, Theorem 1.1 will apply to the collapse of spacelike data more general than those where the scalar field and its gradient have compact support, cf. [7]. on the initial hypersurface 𝒮\mathcal{S}, provided that some additional assumption is made ensuring that the black hole not be extremal in the limit. In particular, the Lorentzian 22-dimensional quotient 𝒬\mathcal{Q} of the future Cauchy development {ℳ,g,Fμ​ν,ϕ}\{\mathcal{M},g,F_{\mu\nu},\phi\} of such data contains a subset 𝒟∪𝒢\mathcal{D}\cup\mathcal{G} with Penrose diagram depicted as the union of the lighter-shaded regions below:

In the above diagram, 𝒟\mathcal{D} is the region of [24], ℋ+\mathcal{H}^{+} is its event horizon, and 𝒞i​n′\mathcal{C}^{\prime}_{in} and 𝒞o​u​t=ℋ+∩J+​(p)\mathcal{C}_{out}=\mathcal{H}^{+}\cap J^{+}(p) and 𝒢\mathcal{G} are as in Theorem 1.1. It follows that 𝒟∪𝒢∪𝒞​ℋ+∪𝒳\mathcal{D}\cup\mathcal{G}\cup\mathcal{CH}^{+}\cup\mathcal{X} represents the quotient manifold of a subset of a proper extension of (ℳ,g)(\mathcal{M},g) to a larger (ℳ~,g~)(\tilde{\mathcal{M}},\tilde{g}), where g~\tilde{g} is a C0C^{0} metric. The null curve 𝒞​ℋ+\mathcal{CH}^{+} is a subset of the quotient of the Cauchy horizon of ℳ\mathcal{M} in ℳ~\tilde{\mathcal{M}}. Thus, the question of the C0C^{0} inextendibility of the future Cauchy development of complete spherically symmetric asymptotically flat spacelike data is now completely resolved in the negative for the Einstein-Maxwell-scalar field equations, i.e. we have the following Corollary of Theorem 1.1

Corollary 1.3.

Strong cosmic censorship, under the formulation of [13], is false for the Einstein-Maxwell-scalar field equations under spherical symmetry.

If the conditions of Theorem 1.2 are satisfied on ℋ+\mathcal{H}^{+} for the collapse of generic spacelike initial data, then the C0C^{0} extensions depicted above will not be C1C^{1}. A weaker version of strong cosmic censorship would then be true. Retrieving the conditions of Theorem 1.2 on the event horizon of the Cauchy development of an appropriate notion of generic spacelike initial data remains thus an important open problem.

As for the question of Price law decay, it should be noted that previously, Stalker and Machedon [30] had obtained bounds similar to (6)(\ref{pioduvato}) for the wave equation on a fixed Schwarzschild or Reissner-Nordström background.

The techniques of this paper are refinements of methods initiated in [22]. Serious new difficulties arise, however, that affect both the qualitative picture and the estimates at our disposal. Since the event horizon and the apparent horizon no longer coincide, one must show that an apparent horizon (and consequently, a trapped region) emerges in evolution. This can be accomplished by using the celebrated “red-shift” effect. (See Section 7. Note that the “red-shift” effect plays a fundamental role in [24] as well.) Another difficulty is that since the initial data are not trapped or marginally trapped, monotonicity special to trapped regions cannot be immediately applied. On the one hand, this implies that the pointwise estimate for one of the controlling quantities used heavily in [22] is here lost, and new arguments must be introduced to circumvent this. On the other hand, an additional argument is also necessary to ensure that the monotonicity of the mass difference, crucial to the proof of blow-up, holds in the trapped region, as this depended on appropriate conditions being met at the apparent horizon66 6 Since in [22], the apparent horizon coincided with the event horizon, these conditions could be imposed directly as an assumption on initial data.. This additional argument is accomplished again employing the red-shift effect.

Besides the novel qualitative features discussed above, the perturbations introduced here differ from those of [22] quantitatively, and this difference persists after the trapped region has formed. We will discuss this further at the end of Section 3. In some sense, this renders the proof of blow-up slightly easier but the proof of stability harder. In particular, the so-called “stable blue-shift region” must be handled with considerably more care. For this, certain B​VBV estimates for the scalar field will prove useful.

Despite these differences, this paper confirms the qualitative picture of the emergence of a “stable red-shift” region, a “no-shift” region, and a sufficiently large “stable blue-shift” region, before the effects of instability become large. It thus supports the thesis of [22] that this picture may indeed represent the interior of black holes that emerge from realistic gravitational collapse.

The outline of this paper is as follows: In Section 2 we present the spherically symmetric Einstein-Maxwell-scalar field equations and in Section 3 we formulate precisely the initial value problem. The definition of the maximal future development, together with an extension theorem involving the area radius rr, are stated in Section 4. Section 5 reviews some of the important monotonicity properties of the equations that are central in the analysis. Section 6 gives an overview of the main ideas employed in proving both stability and blow-up, and more generally, in the analysis of black hole interiors. Stability is then established in the course of Sections 7, 8, 9, 10, and 11. Blow-up is shown in Section 12. Certain a priori B​VBV-estimates for the scalar field ϕ\phi are left to Section 13. Finally, we give in the Appendix two simple causal constructions, to which we will often make reference.

3 The initial value problem

The data considered in [22], expressed in the coordinates of the present paper, are such that θ\theta vanishes initially on the event horizon, and ζ\zeta decays to 00 polynomially in uu on the ingoing segment as u→0u\to 0. Thus, the data defined in this section include in particular the data of [22].1010 10 The more restricted data of Section 12, however, necessary to prove blow up, do not contain the analogous restricted data of Theorem 2 of [22]. One should note that once the solution has evolved up to a spacelike curve beyond the apparent horizon (for instance ΓE\Gamma_{E} of Proposition 7.1), it would be difficult to decide, on the basis of measurements along that curve, whether in the initial data θ\theta vanished on the event horizon or merely decayed exponentially; this is due to the backscattering of radiation. Thus, the data of [22] should be compared more generally with data in which θ\theta decays exponentially. This (exponential vs. polynomial) is the important quantitative difference between the data of [22] and the data considered here.

4 The maximal future development

Recall the subset 𝒦⁡(u0)\mathcal{K}(u_{0}) of the (u,v)(u,v) plane defined in Section 3. |ν−1|(u,v)k−1,|κ|(u,v)k−1,|κ−1|(u,v)k−1,|ϖ|(u,v)k,|θ|(u,v)k−1,|ζ|(u,v)k−1}.\displaystyle\hbox{}\left.|\nu^{-1}|^{k-1}_{(u,v)},|\kappa|^{k-1}_{(u,v)},|\kappa^{-1}|^{k-1}_{(u,v)},|\varpi|^{k}_{(u,v)},|\theta|^{k-1}_{(u,v)},|\zeta|^{k-1}_{(u,v)}\right\}.

Standard techniques (see [15]) then yield the following

Theorem 4.1.

Let kk be an integer k≥1k\geq 1. Let rr, κ\kappa, λ\lambda, ϖ\varpi, θ\theta, ϕ\phi be functions on {0}×[V,∞)\{0\}\times[V,\infty) satisfying (35)(\ref{INITv1})–(50)(\ref{orise}), and let ζ\zeta, ν\nu be functions on [0,u0)×{V}[0,u_{0})\times\{V\} satisfying (51)(\ref{INITu1})–(52)(\ref{INITu2}), and assume that θ⁡(0,v)∈Ck−1\theta(0,v)\in C^{k-1}, ζ⁡(u,V)∈Ck−1\zeta(u,V)\in C^{k-1}. Then there exists a unique non-empty open set

𝒢⁡(u0)⊂𝒦⁡(u0),\mathcal{G}(u_{0})\subset\mathcal{K}(u_{0}),

and unique extensions of the functions rr, λ\lambda, ν\nu, κ\kappa, ϖ\varpi, θ\theta, ζ\zeta, ϕ\phi to 𝒢⁡(u0)\mathcal{G}(u_{0}) such that

  1. 1.

    The functions satisfy (11)(\ref{ruqu})–(14)(\ref{th-orism}), (16)(\ref{puqu})–(20)(\ref{sign2}), and

    |(r,λ,ν,κ,ϖ,θ,ζ)|(u,v)k<∞,|(r,\lambda,\nu,\kappa,\varpi,\theta,\zeta)|^{k}_{(u,v)}<\infty,

    for all (u,v)∈𝒢⁡(u0)(u,v)\in\mathcal{G}(u_{0}).

  2. 2.

    𝒢⁡(u0)\mathcal{G}(u_{0}) is a past subset of 𝒦⁡(u0)\mathcal{K}(u_{0}), i.e. J−​(𝒢⁡(u0))⊂𝒢⁡(u0)J^{-}(\mathcal{G}(u_{0}))\subset\mathcal{G}(u_{0}).

  3. 3.

    For each (u,v)∈∂𝒢⁡(u0)¯(u,v)\in\partial\overline{\mathcal{G}(u_{0})}, we have

    |(r,λ,ν,κ,ϖ,θ,ζ)|(u,v)1=∞.|(r,\lambda,\nu,\kappa,\varpi,\theta,\zeta)|^{1}_{(u,v)}=\infty.

Here 𝒢⁡(u0)¯\overline{\mathcal{G}(u_{0})} denotes the closure of 𝒢⁡(u0)\mathcal{G}(u_{0}) in the topology of 𝒦⁡(u0)\mathcal{K}(u_{0}). The collection

{𝒢⁡(u0),r,λ,ν,κ,ϖ,θ,ζ,ϕ}\{\mathcal{G}(u_{0}),r,\lambda,\nu,\kappa,\varpi,\theta,\zeta,\phi\} (59)

is the so-called maximal future development of the initial data set. By property 3, it follows easily that if θ⁡(0,v)∈Ck~\theta(0,v)\in C^{\tilde{k}}, ζ⁡(u,V)∈Ck~\zeta(u,V)\in C^{\tilde{k}}, for k~>1\tilde{k}>1, then (59)(\ref{suvo9}) does not depend on the value of 1≤k≤k~1\leq k\leq\tilde{k} we fix in Theorem 4.1. Thus, we need not refer explicitly to the value of kk in (59)(\ref{suvo9}).

One should note that in this topology, ∂𝒢⁡(u0)¯=𝒢⁡(u0)¯∖𝒢⁡(u0)\partial\overline{\mathcal{G}(u_{0})}=\overline{\mathcal{G}(u_{0})}\setminus\mathcal{G}(u_{0}) is empty in the case of the Reissner-Nordström solution, i.e. it includes neither the segment {u0}×[V,∞)\{u_{0}\}\times[V,\infty), nor the Cauchy horizon.

One can easily prove that the following result of [22] also holds for the initial data considered here:

Theorem 4.2.

The function rr can be extended continuously to a function on 𝒢⁡(u0)¯\overline{\mathcal{G}(u_{0})}, such that r⁡(p)=0r(p)=0 for all p∈∂𝒢⁡(u0)¯p\in\partial\overline{\mathcal{G}(u_{0})}.

It follows from the above theorem that if p∈𝒢⁡(u0)¯p\in\overline{\mathcal{G}(u_{0})} and r⁡(p)>0r(p)>0, then p∈𝒢⁡(u0)p\in\mathcal{G}(u_{0}). We shall make repeated use of this extension principle in this paper.

Defining g¯\bar{g} on 𝒢⁡(u0)\mathcal{G}(u_{0}) by (7)(\ref{W-orism}), where −Ω2=4​ν​κ-\Omega^{2}=4\nu\kappa, it follows by Proposition 2.1 that from the collection (59)(\ref{suvo9}) we can construct a spherically symmetric solution to (1)(\ref{Einstein-xs})–(4)(\ref{em-xs}). Let us denote this solution by

{ℳ′,g′,Fμ​ν′,ϕ′}.\{\mathcal{M}^{\prime},g^{\prime},F^{\prime}_{\mu\nu},\phi^{\prime}\}. (60)

The solution (60)(\ref{mialusn}) can be proven to be the unique globally hyperbolic solution to the Einstein-Maxwell-scalar field equations (1)(\ref{Einstein-xs})–(4)(\ref{em-xs}), admitting the data, interpreted upstairs, as a suitable “past boundary”. Since ultimately, we are interested here in the characteristic initial value problem only for data which arise from Cauchy data, we will not discuss in detail the issue of uniqueness for this characteristic initial value problem when interpreted upstairs. (See, however, [25].) For data which do arise from Cauchy data, we have, however, the following

Proposition 4.3.

Let {ℳ,g,Fμ​ν,ϕ}\{\mathcal{M},g,F_{\mu\nu},\phi\}, 𝒬\mathcal{Q}, 𝒢′​(u0)\mathcal{G}^{\prime}(u_{0}) be as in Theorem 3.1, and let 𝒢⁡(u0)\mathcal{G}(u_{0}) be as in Theorem 4.1, applied to the functions on {0}×[V,∞)∪[0,u0)×{V}\{0\}\times[V,\infty)\cup[0,u_{0})\times\{V\} given by Theorem 3.1. Then

𝒢′​(u0)=𝒢⁡(u0),\mathcal{G}^{\prime}(u_{0})=\mathcal{G}(u_{0}),

and the functions rr, ν\nu, λ\lambda, ν\nu, κ\kappa, θ\theta, ζ\zeta, ϕ\phi of Theorem 4.1 coincide on 𝒢⁡(u0)\mathcal{G}(u_{0}) with the functions defined in Theorem 3.1.

Proof.

This follows immediately from the uniqueness part of Theorem 4.1, the maximality of the Cauchy development, and the fact that, by the results of [21], the set 𝒢′​(u0)⊂𝒬>0\mathcal{G}^{\prime}(u_{0})\subset\mathcal{Q}^{>0} of Theorem 3.1 satisfies the conditions of Proposition 2.1. ∎

It follows from the above Proposition that statements about (59)(\ref{suvo9}), in the special case where Theorem 4.1 is applied to data arising from Theorem 3.1, are in fact statements about the unique solution to a spacelike Cauchy problem. Moreover, in this case,

𝒢′​(u0)⊂𝒬∖J−​(ℐ+),\mathcal{G}^{\prime}(u_{0})\subset\mathcal{Q}\setminus J^{-}(\mathcal{I}^{+}),

i.e. 𝒢⁡(u0)\mathcal{G}(u_{0}) can be viewed as a subset of the black hole region of an asymptotically flat spacetime. In a slight abuse of notation, we will often refer to 𝒢⁡(u0)\mathcal{G}(u_{0}) as describing black hole region even when it does not arise as above.

In the sequel, we shall consider initial data as having been fixed once and for all. Applying Theorem 4.1, we are given (59)(\ref{suvo9}). We note, however, the following. In the course of the paper, we will restrict attention again and again to sets

D+​([0,U)×{V}∪{0}×[V,∞))∩𝒢⁡(u0)=𝒢⁡(u0)∩𝒦⁡(U)D^{+}([0,U)\times\{V\}\cup\{0\}\times[V,\infty))\cap\mathcal{G}(u_{0})=\mathcal{G}(u_{0})\cap\mathcal{K}(U) (61)

for smaller and smaller U<u0U<u_{0}. This set (61)(\ref{tosuvolo}), together with the restrictions of the functions rr, ν\nu, λ\lambda, κ\kappa, ϖ\varpi, θ\theta, ζ\zeta, ϕ\phi, correspond to the collection (59)(\ref{suvo9}) that emerges from Theorem 4.1 applied to the restriction of the initial data to [0,U)×{V}∪{0}×[V,∞)[0,U)\times\{V\}\cup\{0\}\times[V,\infty). There is thus no confusion if we denote the set (61)(\ref{tosuvolo}) by 𝒢⁡(U)\mathcal{G}(U).

Given UU, keep in mind that there will be three distinct topological and conformal structures which one might want to consider: (𝒢⁡(U),−Ω2​d​u​d​v)(\mathcal{G}(U),-\Omega^{2}dudv), (𝒦⁡(U),−d​u​d​v)(\mathcal{K}(U),-dudv), and the (closed) Penrose diagram 𝒫​𝒟¯\overline{\mathcal{PD}} of the spacetime 𝒢⁡(U)\mathcal{G}(U). The structure of 𝒦⁡(U)\mathcal{K}(U) is convenient for doing analysis, in particular, for formulating Theorems 4.1 and 4.2. The structure of the Penrose diagram 𝒫​𝒟\mathcal{PD} is convenient for global causal geometric statements, like saying that the spacelike curve γ⊂𝒦⁡(U)\gamma\subset\mathcal{K}(U) terminates at i+i^{+} or parametrizing what will be Cauchy horizon 𝒞​ℋ+\mathcal{CH}^{+}. Finally, the structure of (𝒢⁡(U),−Ω2​d​u​d​v)(\mathcal{G}(U),-\Omega^{2}dudv) is fundamental, as it is the structure of our spacetime itself. All three structures coincide when restricted to 𝒢⁡(U)\mathcal{G}(U).

5 Monotonicity

Since ν<0\nu<0 on [0,u0)×{V}[0,u_{0})\times\{V\}, it follows by definition of (58)(\ref{normdef}) that

ν<0\nu<0 (62)

throughout 𝒢⁡(u0)\mathcal{G}(u_{0}). In view of the fact that r⁡(0,v)≤r+r(0,v)\leq r_{+}, integration of (62)(\ref{nmono}) in uu now gives

r≤r+.r\leq r_{+}. (63)

In contrast to ν\nu, the sign of λ\lambda will change in evolution. Define the so-called trapped region 𝒯\mathcal{T} by

𝒯={(u,v)∈𝒢⁡(u0):λ⁡(u,v)<0},\mathcal{T}=\{(u,v)\in\mathcal{G}(u_{0}):\lambda(u,v)<0\},

and the apparent horizon 𝒜\mathcal{A} by

𝒜={(u,v)∈𝒢⁡(u0):λ⁡(u,v)=0}.\mathcal{A}=\{(u,v)\in\mathcal{G}(u_{0}):\lambda(u,v)=0\}.

From (58)(\ref{normdef}), the equation λ=κ⁡(1−μ)\lambda=\kappa(1-\mu), and the fact that κ>0\kappa>0 on {0}×[V,∞)\{0\}\times[V,\infty), it follows that κ\kappa is positive in 𝒢⁡(u0)\mathcal{G}(u_{0}), and that 1−μ⁡(u,v)<01-\mu(u,v)<0 if and only if (u,v)∈𝒯(u,v)\in\mathcal{T}, and 1−μ⁡(u,v)=01-\mu(u,v)=0 if and only if (u,v)∈𝒜(u,v)\in\mathcal{A}.

From (18)(\ref{fdb1}) and (62)(\ref{nmono}), we have

∂uκ≤0.\partial_{u}\kappa\leq 0. (64)

In 𝒯\mathcal{T}, ν1−μ\frac{\nu}{1-\mu} is also a positive quantity, and

∂vν1−μ≤0,\partial_{v}\frac{\nu}{1-\mu}\leq 0, (65)

by (28)(\ref{fdb2}) The above inequality implies that if (u,v)∈𝒜(u,v)\in\mathcal{A}, then (u,v∗)∈𝒜∪𝒯(u,v^{*})\in\mathcal{A}\cup\mathcal{T}, for v∗>vv^{*}>v, while if (u,v)∈𝒯(u,v)\in\mathcal{T}, then (u,v∗)∈𝒯(u,v^{*})\in\mathcal{T} for v∗>vv^{*}>v.

Note that ν1−μ\frac{\nu}{1-\mu} clearly blows up identically on 𝒜\mathcal{A}, so this fraction cannot be immediately utilized as a controlling quantity in 𝒯\mathcal{T}, except in the case where 𝒜\mathcal{A} coincides with the event horizon. (Compare with [22] where one did have a priori pointwise bounds for ν1−μ\frac{\nu}{1-\mu} throughout 𝒢⁡(u0)\mathcal{G}(u_{0}), on account of our special choice of initial data!)

Finally, in view of the above and (16)(\ref{puqu}) and (17)(\ref{pvqu}), it is clear that we have the following additional monotonicity in 𝒯\mathcal{T}:

∂vϖ≥0,∂uϖ≥0.\partial_{v}\varpi\geq 0,\partial_{u}\varpi\geq 0. (66)

We note here that the inequalities of this section, with the exception of (66)(\ref{spemov}), are quite general, and depend only on the dominant energy condition. This is nicely discussed in [14]. We shall return to the issue of monotonicity in Section 12, where, in particular, we shall be able to prove, for appropriate initial data, the inequality ∂u∂vϖ≥0\partial_{u}\partial_{v}\varpi\geq 0, in 𝒯\mathcal{T}.

6 Remarks on the analysis of black holes

Before beginning the study of our system, it will be useful to make a few preliminary remarks that will give a taste of the special flavor of the analysis of (16)(\ref{puqu})–(20)(\ref{sign2}) in black hole regions. In addition to providing an outline of the approach taken in the following sections, these remarks may be relevant for understanding more general charged or rotating black holes.

In view of Theorem 4.2, to delimit the extent of the maximal domain of development, it is enough to control (from below!) rr. The function rr would indeed be controlled if we could appropriately bound its null derivatives, let us say ν\nu. But integrating equation (26)(\ref{nqu}), one deduces that it is the following quantity that must then be controlled:

∫v1v22​κr2​(ϖ−e2r)​𝑑v.\int_{v_{1}}^{v_{2}}{\frac{2\kappa}{r^{2}}\left(\varpi-\frac{e^{2}}{r}\right)dv}. (67)

In the Reissner-Nordström solution, where ϕ≡0\phi\equiv 0, θ≡0\theta\equiv 0, ζ≡0\zeta\equiv 0, it follows by (18)(\ref{fdb1}) that

∂uκ=0,\partial_{u}\kappa=0,

and thus, by (35)(\ref{INITv1}), ∫v1v2κ​𝑑v=v2−v1\int_{v_{1}}^{v_{2}}\kappa dv=v_{2}-v_{1}. This means that as v2→∞v_{2}\to\infty, the integral (67)(\ref{apeiro;}) blows up in the trapped region1111 11 It is instructive to compare with the domain of outer communications 𝒟\mathcal{D} of [24]. There, as v2→∞v_{2}\to\infty, r→∞r\to\infty, and this keeps the integral bounded. In the trapped region, on the other hand, we have the a priori upper bound (63)(\ref{*IKI*}) for rr. for all values of uu. For fixed u>0u>0, the sign of (ϖ−e2r)\left(\varpi-\frac{e^{2}}{r}\right), however, becomes negative as v→∞v\to\infty. Thus the effect of (67)(\ref{apeiro;}) in integrating (26)(\ref{nqu}) is to make ν\nu tend to 00 in the limit as 𝒞​ℋ+\mathcal{CH^{+}} is approached. The negative sign for (ϖ−e2r)\left(\varpi-\frac{e^{2}}{r}\right) is thus “favorable” for controlling rr. We will call this the blue-shift sign.

If we examine, however, the sign of (ϖ−e2r)\left(\varpi-\frac{e^{2}}{r}\right) on {0}×[V,∞)∪[0,u0)×{V}\{0\}\times[V,\infty)\cup[0,u_{0})\times\{V\}, we find that it is positive. This is the “unfavorable” sign for the control of rr, and we will call it the red-shift sign.

From this point of view, key to the formation of the Cauchy horizon is the fact that (ϖ−e2r)\left(\varpi-\frac{e^{2}}{r}\right) changes sign in evolution from red-shift to blue-shift1212 12 We see that in the case e=0e=0, such a change of sign is impossible; this explains in particular why the Schwarzschild solution behaves so differently from the Reissner-Nordström solution., and moreover, that this blue-shift region ℬ\mathcal{B} is sufficiently large, so as to “compensate” for the effect of the red-shift region ℛ\mathcal{R}, which in the meantime has made |ν||\nu| large.

In order to understand better the significance of (67)(\ref{apeiro;}), it is useful to separate out a region where (67)(\ref{apeiro;}) can be uniformly bounded. We will call such regions “no-shift” regions, and denoted them 𝒩\mathcal{N}. The precise boundary of any such region is a bit arbitrary, but nonetheless, the concept is useful. The Reissner-Nordström solution can be decomposed as follows:

The above picture is our starting point for understanding the evolution of the initial value problem considered here. The partition into red-shift, no-shift, and blue-shift regions will be key to understanding analytically the various quantities of our system.

We have already seen in the discussion above the different effects on rr in each of the three regions. But these regions also have very different effects on ϖ\varpi. We turn now to examine this point.

In the Reissner-Nordström solution, the scalar field vanishes, and thus ϖ\varpi is constant. With a scalar field present, however, (16)(\ref{puqu}) implies that, all other things being equal, the smaller the value of |ν||\nu|, the larger the value of ∂uϖ\partial_{u}\varpi. Thus, the red-shift sign, which was unfavorable for the control of rr, is favorable for the control of ϖ\varpi, while the blue-shift sign, which was favorable for rr, is unfavorable for ϖ\varpi.

The fact that the blue-shift sign is “unfavorable” for ϖ\varpi is basically what led to the conjecture of strong cosmic censorship in the first place. We will return to this issue shortly. Let us first try to understand the strategy employed for proving the stability result, Theorem 1.1.

As noted earlier, key to the Reissner-Nordström behavior of rr is the blue-shift region. Yet, with the hindsight of our result, namely that ϖ→∞\varpi\to\infty as v→∞v\to\infty, one does not have the blue-shift sign sufficiently close to 𝒞​ℋ+\mathcal{CH}^{+} in the topology of the Penrose diagram. The best one can hope for, then, is to have at least a sufficiently large piece of blue shift region ℬ\mathcal{B}, somewhere. As we shall see, the whole situation is quite delicate. An outline of the complete argument is as follows:

  1. 1.

    In Section 7, we shall define what will be a redshift region ℛ=J−​(ΓE)\mathcal{R}=J^{-}(\Gamma_{E}), and we shall show that ℛ\mathcal{R} contains an achronal apparent horizon 𝒜\mathcal{A}. Using the red-shift sign of (67)(\ref{apeiro;}), we will be able to bound all quantities in ℛ\mathcal{R}. The future boundary of ℛ\mathcal{R} will be a spacelike curve ΓE⊂𝒯\Gamma_{E}\subset\mathcal{T}, on which ϖ−e2r=E>0\varpi-\frac{e^{2}}{r}=E>0.

  2. 2.

    Next, in Section 8, we shall define what will be a no-shift region 𝒩=J+​(ΓE)∩J−​(Γ−ξ)\mathcal{N}=J^{+}(\Gamma_{E})\cap J^{-}(\Gamma_{-\xi}). Again, we shall be able to bound all quantities in 𝒩\mathcal{N}, using the uniform boundedness of (67)(\ref{apeiro;}). In particular, λ∼1\lambda\sim 1, κ∼1\kappa\sim 1, ϖ∼ϖ+\varpi\sim\varpi_{+}. On the spacelike curve Γ−ξ\Gamma_{-\xi}, we will have ϖ−e2r=−ξ<0\varpi-\frac{e^{2}}{r}=-\xi<0. The sign has turned blue-shift!

  3. 3.

    In Section 9, we shall define what will be a blue-shift region ℬγ=J+​(Γ−ξ)∩J−​(γ)\mathcal{B}_{\gamma}=J^{+}(\Gamma_{-\xi})\cap J^{-}(\gamma). Understanding the vv-dimensions of this region will be fundamental. On the one hand, ℬγ\mathcal{B}_{\gamma} will be small enough to allow us to control all quantities, by playing off the decay rate of the scalar field with the the rate in which (67)(\ref{apeiro;}) blows up. In particular, κ∼1\kappa\sim 1, ϖ∼ϖ+\varpi\sim\varpi_{+}. On the other hand, ℬγ\mathcal{B}_{\gamma} will be large enough so as to have a suitable “moderating” effect on λ=∂vr\lambda=\partial_{v}r.1313 13 An important technical point in this paper is how to relate (67)(\ref{apeiro;}), which is log⁡ν⁡(u,v2)−log⁡ν⁡(u,v1)\log\nu(u,v_{2})-\log\nu(u,v_{1}), with an analogous expression for λ\lambda. It turns out that pointwise estimates are more natural for λ\lambda than for ν\nu because of the stability of κ=λ⁡(1−μ)\kappa=\lambda(1-\mu). Specifically, on the curve γ\gamma, we will show

    λ⁡(u|γ​(v),v)≤C​v−s\lambda(u|_{\gamma}(v),v)\leq Cv^{-s} (68)

    for an s>1s>1. The significance of s>1s>1 is that (68)(\ref{stagrngora}) can be integrated in vv.

  4. 4.

    We will show in Section 10 that if there are regions in J+​(γ)J^{+}(\gamma) where the sign of (67)(\ref{apeiro;}) becomes red-shift, then (67)(\ref{apeiro;}) is uniformly bounded in those regions, i.e. J+​(γ)J^{+}(\gamma) can be decomposed into blue-shift and no-shift regions. Either way, a bound (68)(\ref{stagrngora}) of the form is preserved. This allows us to bound rr a priori away from 00 in 𝒢⁡(U)\mathcal{G}(U), for sufficiently small UU. It will follow by Theorem 4.2 that 𝒢⁡(U)=𝒦⁡(U)\mathcal{G}(U)=\mathcal{K}(U).

  5. 5.

    Finally, estimating suitable quantities in 𝒢⁡(𝒰)\mathcal{G(U)}, we will be able to show in Section 11, that g¯\bar{g}, rr, and ϕ\phi can be extended continuously to 𝒞​ℋ+\mathcal{CH}^{+}, completing the proof of Theorem 1.1.

The various curves and regions referred to in the above outline are depicted below:

We now turn to discuss the blow-up of ϖ\varpi. Again, the key is the blue-shift region, which tends to make ϖ\varpi large. Yet, as noted earlier, the growing of ϖ\varpi tends to limit the strength of, and eventually completely destroy, the blue-shift region. It seems that we have to face the uncertain competition between these two effects in the potentially unstable part of the blue-shift region, ℬ∩J+​(γ)\mathcal{B}\cap J^{+}(\gamma). Our argument proceeds by contradiction. There are two steps:

  1. 1.

    It is shown that for appropriate initial data, the following dichotomy holds: Either the solution in J+​(γ)J^{+}(\gamma) is “qualitatively similar” to the Reissner-Nordström solution in ℬ\mathcal{B}, or ϖ\varpi blows up identically on 𝒞​ℋ+\mathcal{CH}^{+}. The phrase “qualitatively similar” means in particular that the sign of (67)(\ref{apeiro;}) should remain blue-shift, ϖ\varpi should extend to a finite-valued function on 𝒞​ℋ+\mathcal{CH}^{+} with ϖ⁡(q)→ϖ+\varpi(q)\to\varpi_{+} as q→i+q\to i^{+}, and λ\lambda should decay exponentially in vv for fixed uu. The arguments proving this dichotomy rely heavily on the strong monotonicity properties proven in Section 12.

  2. 2.

    By step 1, if ϖ\varpi does not blow up, we can assume that the solution in J+​(γ)J^{+}(\gamma) is indeed “qualitatively similar” to Reissner-Nordström in the sense described above. But this implies that the linear mechanism for blow-up should apply. Indeed, the blue-shift factor (67)(\ref{apeiro;}) operates, making ϖ\varpi large, contradicting in particular the assumption that ϖ⁡(q)→ϖ+\varpi(q)\to\varpi_{+}. Thus, ϖ\varpi blows up after all.

The proof of step 2 can be considered a linear theory argument1414 14 Indeed, this computation shows a form of blow up for the decoupled problem as well. that should be compared with Chandrasekhar and Hartle [9], even though, with the help of the monotonicity proven in Section 12, we will be able to derive it almost immediately. In this sense, the linear theory that was responsible for the original conjecture of strong cosmic censorship indeed finds its way in the present proof, albeit as a part of a contradiction argument.

7 The red-shift region

Recalling the inequality (32)(\ref{alloxipriv}), one can choose a positive constant EE such that

ϖ+−e2r+−2​(K~+M~)<E<ϖ+−e2r+−32​(K~+M~).\varpi_{+}-\frac{e^{2}}{r_{+}}-2(\tilde{K}+\tilde{M})<E<\varpi_{+}-\frac{e^{2}}{r_{+}}-\frac{3}{2}(\tilde{K}+\tilde{M}). (69)

ℛ={(u,v)∈𝒢⁡(u0):(ϖ−e2r)​(u~,v~)>E​for​all​(u~,v~)∈J−​(u,v)}.\mathcal{R}=\left\{(u,v)\in\mathcal{G}(u_{0}):\left(\varpi-\frac{e^{2}}{r}\right)(\tilde{u},\tilde{v})>E{\rm\ for\ all\ }(\tilde{u},\tilde{v})\in J^{-}(u,v)\right\}.

≤\displaystyle\leq Λ​e2r0​r+​(2​p−1)​v−2​p+1\displaystyle\frac{\Lambda e^{2}}{r_{0}r_{+}(2p-1)}v^{-2p+1}

it follows that ℛ\mathcal{R} is a non-empty subset of 𝒢⁡(u0)\mathcal{G}(u_{0}). By continuity, ℛ\mathcal{R} contains some open set (in the topology of 𝒦⁡(u0)\mathcal{K}(u_{0})) containing {0}×[V,∞)\{0\}\times[V,\infty). As ℛ\mathcal{R} is clearly a past set, its future boundary ΓE\Gamma_{E}, given by

ΓE=ℛ¯∩I+​(ℛ)∩𝒢⁡(u0)∖ℛ,\Gamma_{E}=\overline{\mathcal{R}}\cap I^{+}(\mathcal{R})\cap\mathcal{G}(u_{0})\setminus\mathcal{R},

is a (possibly empty) achronal curve.

Step 1 of the outline of Section 6 is accomplished by the following

Proposition 7.1.

For U1U_{1} sufficiently small, ΓE∩𝒢⁡(U1)≠∅\Gamma_{E}\cap\mathcal{G}(U_{1})\neq\emptyset is spacelike and terminates at i+i^{+}. Moreover, on ΓE∩𝒢⁡(U1)\Gamma_{E}\cap\mathcal{G}(U_{1}), the equality

ϖ−e2r=E\varpi-\frac{e^{2}}{r}=E

holds identically, and ΓE∩𝒢⁡(U1)⊂𝒯\Gamma_{E}\cap\mathcal{G}(U_{1})\subset\mathcal{T}:

Finally, as depicted in the above Penrose diagram, 𝒜∩𝒢⁡(U1)\mathcal{A}\cap\mathcal{G}(U_{1}) is achronal, and

𝒯∩𝒢⁡(U1)=I+​(𝒜)∩𝒢⁡(U1).\mathcal{T}\cap\mathcal{G}(U_{1})=I^{+}(\mathcal{A})\cap\mathcal{G}(U_{1}).
Proof.

The proof will proceed by a bootstrap argument. We first define a region ℛ~\tilde{\mathcal{R}} as the set of points (u,v)∈𝒢⁡(u0)(u,v)\in\mathcal{G}(u_{0}) such that the following estimates hold for all (u~,v~)⊂J−​(u,v)(\tilde{u},\tilde{v})\subset J^{-}(u,v):

(ϖ−e2r)​(u~,v~)>E,\left(\varpi-\frac{e^{2}}{r}\right)(\tilde{u},\tilde{v})>E, (71)
r⁡(u~,v~)>c12,r(\tilde{u},\tilde{v})>\frac{c_{1}}{2}, (72)
|1−μ⁡(u~,v~)|<2​M1,|1-\mu(\tilde{u},\tilde{v})|<2M_{1}, (73)
|ζν|​(u~,v~)<3​C~​r+2E​c1​v~−p,\left|\frac{\zeta}{\nu}\right|(\tilde{u},\tilde{v})<\frac{3\tilde{C}r_{+}^{2}}{Ec_{1}}\tilde{v}^{-p}, (74)
|θ⁡(u~,v~)|<C~​v~−p,|\theta(\tilde{u},\tilde{v})|<\tilde{C}\tilde{v}^{-p}, (75)

for c1c_{1}, M1M_{1} given by (29)(\ref{c_1ori}) and (30)(\ref{M1ori}), and C~\tilde{C} defined by

C~=max⁡{2​c1​Er+2​C¯​eV​Er+2​e−p​(p​r+2E)p,3​C}.\tilde{C}=\max\left\{\frac{2c_{1}E}{r_{+}^{2}}\overline{C}e^{V\frac{E}{r_{+}^{2}}}e^{-p}\left(\frac{pr_{+}^{2}}{E}\right)^{p},3C\right\}. (76)

In ℛ~¯∩𝒢⁡(U1)\overline{\tilde{\mathcal{R}}}\cap\mathcal{G}(U_{1}), we shall be able to retrieve, in fact improve the bounds (74)(\ref{booteva}), (75)(\ref{bootduo}), (72)(\ref{BS2}), and (73)(\ref{BS3}), for U1U_{1} sufficiently small. A simple continuity argument will then imply that ℛ~∩𝒢⁡(U1)=ℛ∩𝒢⁡(U1)\tilde{\mathcal{R}}\cap\mathcal{G}(U_{1})=\mathcal{R}\cap\mathcal{G}(U_{1}).

The estimates (74)(\ref{booteva}), (75)(\ref{bootduo}) thus obtained will easily lead to the remaining conclusions of the proposition.

Before giving the details of the proof, it might be useful to point out in advance some of the main points. We will see that our bootstrap assumptions above imply

e∫Vv2​κr2​(ϖ−e2r)≥eH​v,e^{\int_{V}^{v}{\frac{2\kappa}{r^{2}}\left(\varpi-\frac{e^{2}}{r}\right)}}\geq e^{Hv}, (77)

for some positive constant HH. Integrating the equation (85)(\ref{integrating}), and playing off the above exponential factor (77)(\ref{masdivei}), one can transfer the polynomial decay (75)(\ref{bootduo}) of θ\theta in vv into similar decay (74)(\ref{booteva}) of ζν\frac{\zeta}{\nu}. This is the heart of the red-shift technique.

As far as retrieving the bootstrap assumptions is concerned, we note in advance three sources for a smallness factor:

  1. 1.

8 A “no-shift” region

Proposition 7.1 has successfully brought us into the trapped region 𝒯\mathcal{T}. The importance of the large contribution of the red-shift factor in the analysis is clear. In this section, we shall investigate a region 𝒩⊂J+​(ΓE)\mathcal{N}\subset J^{+}(\Gamma_{E}), where (67)(\ref{apeiro;}) will be bounded. This will thus be a no-shift region, in the terminology of Section 6. In 𝒩\mathcal{N}, the sign of ϖ−e2r\varpi-\frac{e^{2}}{r} will change from red-shift to blue-shift. 𝒩\mathcal{N} will thus bring us into the blueshift region ℬ\mathcal{B} which we shall investigate in the next section.

Let r−r_{-} denote the smaller root r−=ϖ+−ϖ+2−e2r_{-}=\varpi_{+}-\sqrt{\varpi_{+}^{2}-e^{2}} of the quadratic equation r2−2​ϖ+​r+e2=0r^{2}-2\varpi_{+}r+e^{2}=0.1616 16 This is the constant value of rr on the Reissner-Nordström Cauchy horizon. Choosing ξ\xi such that

we define our no-shift region 𝒩\mathcal{N} as follows:

is a (possibly empty) achronal curve.

We have

Proposition 8.1.

For 0<U20<U_{2} sufficiently small, Γ−ξ∩𝒢⁡(U2)≠∅\Gamma_{-\xi}\cap\mathcal{G}(U_{2})\neq\emptyset, and is a nonempty spacelike curve terminating at i+i^{+}. Moreover, on Γ−ξ∩𝒢⁡(U2)\Gamma_{-\xi}\cap\mathcal{G}(U_{2}), the equality

ϖ−e2r=−ξ\varpi-\frac{e^{2}}{r}=-\xi

holds identically.

Proof.

Again, we prove this Proposition by a bootstrap argument. We consider a region 𝒩~\tilde{\mathcal{N}} defined as the set of (u,v)∈𝒩(u,v)\in\mathcal{N} such that for all (u~,v~)∈J−​(u~,v~)∩𝒩(\tilde{u},\tilde{v})\in J^{-}(\tilde{u},\tilde{v})\cap\mathcal{N}, the inequalities

v~−v|ΓE​(u~)<H,\tilde{v}-v|_{\Gamma_{E}}(\tilde{u})<H, (97)
ϖ⁡(u~,v~)<Π\varpi(\tilde{u},\tilde{v})<\Pi (98)

hold, for constants HH, Π\Pi to be determined below. By the previous proposition, 𝒩~\tilde{\mathcal{N}} is nonempty, provided Π>ϖ+\Pi>\varpi_{+}. We will show that in 𝒩~¯∩𝒩∩𝒢⁡(U2)\overline{\tilde{\mathcal{N}}}\cap\mathcal{N}\cap\mathcal{G}(U_{2}), for small enough U2U_{2}, assumptions (97)(\ref{nBS4}) and (98)(\ref{nBS5}) can in fact be improved, for appropriate choice of HH, Π\Pi. It will follow by a continuity argument that 𝒩~∩𝒢⁡(U2)=𝒩∩𝒢⁡(U2)\tilde{\mathcal{N}}\cap\mathcal{G}(U_{2})=\mathcal{N}\cap\mathcal{G}(U_{2}). The bounds obtained in 𝒩~\tilde{\mathcal{N}} will easily imply the assertion of the proposition.

Again, before giving the details of the proof, it might be useful to point out some of the key points. The bootstrap assumption (97)(\ref{nBS4}) together with (64)(\ref{F1}) implies in particular a bound for ∫κ​𝑑v\int\kappa dv, when the integral is taken in 𝒩~\tilde{\mathcal{N}}, hence the no-shift property of 𝒩\mathcal{N}. Estimates for the scalar field derivatives θ\theta and ζ\zeta in this section are derived from the Propositions of Section 13; a discussion of these is deferred till then. a contradiction.

The second statement of the proposition now follows immediately from (19)(\ref{sign1}) and (20)(\ref{sign2}). ∎

Corollary 12.3.

Under the assumptions of Proposition 12.2, ∂u∂vϖ≥0\partial_{u}\partial_{v}\varpi\geq 0 in D+​(γ~)∩𝒢⁡(u0)D^{+}(\tilde{\gamma})\cap\mathcal{G}(u_{0}). by the previous Proposition and the monotonicity (64)(\ref{F1}) satisfied by κ\kappa. The second statement of the theorem follows by integration of this inequality in 𝒳\mathcal{X}. ∎

Note that for γ~=𝒜∩𝒢⁡(U1)\tilde{\gamma}=\mathcal{A}\cap\mathcal{G}(U_{1}), D+​(γ~)∩𝒢⁡(u0)=J+​(𝒜∩𝒢⁡(U1))D^{+}(\tilde{\gamma})\cap\mathcal{G}(u_{0})=J^{+}(\mathcal{A}\cap\mathcal{G}(U_{1})).

We can now state the theorem of this section.

Theorem 12.4.

For initial data satisfying (149)(\ref{yenidurum}), ϖ\varpi blows up identically in the limit on the Cauchy horizon 𝒞​ℋ+\mathcal{CH}^{+} for 0<u<U40<u<U_{4}, i.e.

limv→∞ϖ⁡(u,v)=∞.\lim_{v\to\infty}\varpi(u,v)=\infty.

The general two-step structure of this proof was outlined in Section 6. But in fact, all the work is in step 1. Step 2, as we shall see, is basically line (160)(\ref{part2}).

Recall that the goal of step 1 is to prove that if the mass does not blow up identically, then the spacetime “looks like” Reissner-Nordström, in the sense discussed in Section 6.

The outline of step 1 is roughly as follows. The proof of the theorem thus reduces to showing that the assumption (151)(\ref{ya}) leads to a contradiction. If θ\theta initially decays exponentially, but there is also an appropriate exponential lower bound on θ\theta, a similar theorem can in fact be proven. To obtain the best results, one has to be slightly more careful with the constants connected to the ∼\sim in the chain of estimates above. Compare with Section 10 or [22].

Heuristic analysis [26, 35, 1, 2] and numerical studies [27, 8] suggest that the “non-oscillatory” behavior that we have assumed in the limit (149)(\ref{yenidurum}) is indeed to be expected, at least for the neutral massless scalar field considered here. As this is not likely to be true for more general matter, and in any case has not been proved even for this matter, it would be nice if assumption (149)(\ref{yenidurum}) could in fact be weakened.

Appendix A Two causal constructions

Let γ~\tilde{\gamma} be a spacelike curve in 𝒦⁡(u0)\mathcal{K}(u_{0}) terminating at i+i^{+}. Suppose (u′,v′)∈γ~(u^{\prime},v^{\prime})\in\tilde{\gamma}. Refer to the Penrose diagram below:

It follows that for all v≥v′v\geq v^{\prime}, there is a unique uu such that (u,v)∈γ~(u,v)\in\tilde{\gamma}. We will use the notation u=u|γ~​(v)u=u|_{\tilde{\gamma}(v)}. Similarly, for u≤u′u\leq u^{\prime}, there is a unique vv such that (u,v)∈γ~(u,v)\in\tilde{\gamma}, and we will write v=v|γ~​(u)v=v|_{\tilde{\gamma}}(u). The latter can clearly be defined even if γ~\tilde{\gamma} is assumed only to be achronal.

We shall make use several times of the following construction: Given two spacelike curves γ~\tilde{\gamma}, γ~′\tilde{\gamma}^{\prime}, terminating at i+i^{+}, with γ~′⊂I+​(γ~)\tilde{\gamma}^{\prime}\subset I^{+}(\tilde{\gamma}), and a point (u,v)(u,v) such that v|γ~​(u)v|_{\tilde{\gamma}(u)}, v|γ~′​(u)v|_{\tilde{\gamma}^{\prime}(u)}, u|γ~​(v)u|_{\tilde{\gamma}(v)}, and v|γ~′​(u)v|_{\tilde{\gamma}^{\prime}(u)} are defined, the (γ~,γ~′,u,v)(\tilde{\gamma},\tilde{\gamma}^{\prime},u,v)-zigzag will be defined as the union

⋃i=1I−1{ui}×[vi,vi+1]∪[ui+1,ui]×{vi+1}\bigcup_{i=1}^{I-1}\{u_{i}\}\times[v_{i},v_{i+1}]\cup[u_{i+1},u_{i}]\times\{v_{i+1}\}

where u1=u¯u_{1}=\bar{u}, v1=v|γ~​(u¯)v_{1}=v|_{\tilde{\gamma}(\bar{u})}, and uiu_{i}, viv_{i} are defined inductively by

vi+1=min⁡{v|γ~′​(u¯),v¯}v_{i+1}=\min\{v|_{\tilde{\gamma}^{\prime}(\bar{u})},\bar{v}\}
ui+1=u|γ~​(vi+1),u_{i+1}=u|_{\tilde{\gamma}(v_{i+1})},

and II is defined to be the first ii such that vi=v¯v_{i}=\bar{v}. Refer to the Penrose diagram below:
